answer: The registration of title to every land parcel under the Act must be “in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applied here, the parcel’s registration of title must follow that cadastral map.

The rule is that, when the Commissioner of Title Settlement receives certified copies of cadastral maps, he must publish a Notice in the Gazette. That Notice must call for any claimants to the land parcel specified in the Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of the Notice. After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must cause an investigation to be conducted to determine the genuinness or otherwise of those claims.

The Act provides two different procedures.

1. **Reference of disputed claims for investigation and determination:** If, during the course of investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because of the disputed nature of the claims, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination to the District Court** having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. This is a **Commissioner-initiated reference** made during the investigations. [node_id: 21-1998/section-21]

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant:** Any claimant aggrieved by any Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 **may prefer an appeal against such declaration within the prescribed period to the District Court** having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. This is a **claimant-initiated appeal** made after the declaration, and it must be filed within the prescribed period. [node_id: 21-1998/section-22]

So, the disputed claims are referred by the Commissioner for determination during the investigation stage, whereas the dissatisfied claimant challenges the declaration by appeal after the declaration has been made.

Under the Registration of Title Act, a person acquiring an interest in a registered land parcel is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered: “No person acquiring an interest in any land parcel registered under the provisions of this Act shall be entitled to such title or interest unless such title or interest is registered under the provisions of this Act.” Also, a registered land parcel or any interest in it “shall be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and every disposition otherwise effected shall be void.” An instrument relating to land “shall take effect on registration” of that instrument under the Act.

Applied here, Nimal’s instrument was not registered under the Act. Therefore the transferee did not acquire the interest, and the private agreement alone did not make the transfer effective. The instrument would take legal effect only upon registration under the Act.

The governing rule is that, “Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.”

Applied to the facts, the instrument is one that purports to convey a registered land parcel to two purchasers “as owners in common.” On the statutory text given, such an instrument is void and shall not be registered, unless it is made in accordance with some other provision of the Act, which is not shown in the supplied material.

The rule is that, for land or land parcels registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) “shall not apply,” and the Partition Act also “shall not apply.”

Applied to the facts: the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, the Prescription Ordinance does not apply to that parcel, so a claim of ownership through prescription is not available under the supplied provision. The Partition Act also does not apply to that parcel, so a partition action concerning that parcel is not permitted under the supplied provision.

The statutory rule is that, once the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and this Act, he shall certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General and then: (a) file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title; and (b) forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the owner’s application to the appropriate Registrar of Title. [21-1998/section-51, 21-1998/section-51/paragraph-a, 21-1998/section-51/paragraph-b]

If the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the application conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and this Act, he shall: (a) file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File; (b) open a new title register in respect of each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross references to that register in the register in which the land parcel is registered; (c) record in the Property Section of the register pertaining to the land parcel that the land comprised therein consists only of common property; (d) record in the Encumbrances Section that registers in respect of condominium parcels have been opened; (e) inform the applicant that the condominium parcels have been registered and notify him of the reference numbers of the relevant registers; and (f) issue a Certificate of Title after recovery of the prescribed fees. [21-1998/section-52, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-a, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-b, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-c, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-d, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-e, 21-1998/section-52/paragraph-f]

The statutory rule is:
- If a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, the surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property. (s 22)
- Subject to that spouse’s half, the next order of inheritance is descendants. (s 23)
- Among descendants, children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation. (s 24)

Applied here:
1. The surviving spouse takes one-half of the estate.
2. The remaining one-half goes to descendants.
3. There are two descendant branches: one living child, and one deceased child represented by two grandchildren.
4. The remaining one-half is divided per stirpes into 2 equal branch shares:
   - one branch for the living child = 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate
   - one branch for the deceased child’s issue = 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate
5. The two grandchildren share their branch equally, so each grandchild gets 1/2 of 1/4 = 1/8 of the whole estate.

So the shares are:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

Order of succession: spouse first takes one-half; the balance then passes to descendants, with representation for the children of the deceased child.

The governing rule is that “[e]very will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka containing any devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka,” if it has been “duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed,” and is made by a person who “by the law of such country or of Sri Lanka [is] competent to make a will,” “shall be valid and effectual to alienate and pass the property” in that immovable property. Here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country where it was executed, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. On those facts, the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in proceedings or an action for enforcing a right of pre-emption, proof must be furnished to the court that the proceedings or action have been registered as a lis pendens in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. [59-1947/section-10]

If the court considers it appropriate as proof of the plaintiff’s bona fides, it may order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount stated in the notice given under section 5. [59-1947/section-11]

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period the court allows, or within any further periods allowed not exceeding three months in the aggregate, the action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases. [59-1947/section-11]

The rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” The Act came into operation on 11 December 1957, and that day is “the appointed day.”

Applied here, the owner mortgages a physically divided portion of a tea estate as a separate lot after the appointed day. That is a mortgage of “a part of a tea… estate as a divided lot” effected on or after the appointed day. Therefore, the mortgage is null and void.

If the condominium parcel itself is transferred, “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel” even if the deed does not specifically mention that share. So the common-elements share goes with the parcel automatically on transfer.

The statutory rule is: “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.”

Applied to the facts, the property is land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan. Because of that, the Partition Law does not apply to that property, so proceedings under the Partition Law cannot be brought in respect of it.

Section 13 says that no plan or map, or copy or tracing of a plan or map, is receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless it satisfies the statutory preparation and certification requirement. The supplied text states one route as follows: it must have been "prepared ... by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him" and "certified by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose". The supplied text also states another certification route: "and certified by a registered licensed surveyor." Applying that rule, the land plan can be received in evidence only if it falls within the stated statutory preparation and certification requirements; otherwise it is not receivable.

Yes. A cadastral map, plan, or any other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, when it purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or any officer acting on his behalf, “shall be admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It also “may be taken as prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original” until evidence to the contrary is given. So, on these facts, the copy is admissible in place of the original, and its initial evidential status is prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated in it. The provision also says it is not necessary to prove that it was in fact signed or authenticated by the Surveyor-General or such officer, or that it is a true copy, or that the facts reflected in it are accurate, until evidence to the contrary is first given.

Rule: "it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares" unless "a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company". So, on these facts, the company may not register the voluntary transfer if no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered. Exception: "nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder or debenture holder, any person to whom the right of any shares in or debentures of the company has been transmitted by operation of law." Therefore, if entitlement to the shares passes by operation of law, the company’s power to register that person as shareholder is preserved despite the lack of an instrument of transfer.

Under Companies Act, s 79, a certificate “signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder” is “prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares.” Applied here, if the certificate was signed in the company’s name by a director and the secretary and specifies the shares held by the person recorded as a shareholder, that certificate is prima facie evidence that the shareholder has title to those shares. It is evidence of title, but only on a prima facie basis.

The statutory duties are:

1. Under Companies Act s 188, a director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes … the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” On the facts, the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so this duty is breached.

2. Under Companies Act s 189(a), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” On the facts, the director carried out the decision recklessly, so this duty is breached.

3. Under Companies Act s 189(b), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” On the facts, the director acted without exercising the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that director’s knowledge and experience, so this duty is breached.

The statutory rule is that “Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.” Applied here, because the transfer of land was completed in direct contravention of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, that alienation is void and has no effect in law.
